blocks.text: Imaging methods that use ionising radiation rely on how radiation interacts with matter: as photons pass through tissue they may be absorbed or scattered, and the pattern of energy deposited and attenuated produces measurable signals at a detector. In nuclear medicine the radiation starts inside the patient, from an administered radiopharmaceutical, so the signal shows how the body is working (function) rather than only its shape (anatomy). In single photon emission computed tomography (SPECT), a gamma-emitting tracer is introduced into the body and a rotating gamma camera records many views, which are reconstructed into cross-sectional images of tracer distribution, giving 3D information about blood flow and organ function.

Positron emission tomography (PET) extends this idea using positron-emitting tracers (Fig 20.10 shows a PET scanner). A small amount of radioactive tracer is injected into a vein; the blood carries it, and it builds up more in very active tissues, such as many cancers and working parts of the brain and heart. As the unstable nuclei of the tracer decay they emit positrons. Each positron travels only a short distance before meeting an electron in nearby tissue; the two annihilate, and their mass is converted into two gamma-ray photons that move in opposite directions. A ring of detectors around the patient detects these photon pairs in coincidence (arriving at the same instant) and sends the signals to a computer, which locates each event on the line joining the two detectors and constructs an image showing where the tracer has collected (Fig 20.11). Brighter areas show higher tracer concentration and therefore higher tissue activity.

blocks.alt: Left (CT): a ring around a patient lying on a couch, with an X-ray source at several positions around the ring and dashed beams crossing the body to detectors opposite; a curved arrow shows the tube rotating; below, a stack of thin slices labelled 2D slices stacked into a 3D image. Right (PET): a ring of detectors around the patient; from a point inside the body a dashed line runs in opposite directions to two red detectors, showing two gamma rays detected at the same instant.
blocks.caption: CT scanning and PET coincidence detection (original diagram after Figs 20.8 to 20.11).
blocks.long_description: CT shines X-rays through the body from outside at many angles and reconstructs each slice. PET instead detects gamma rays coming from a tracer inside the body, two at a time, to map where the tracer has gathered.

blocks.text: So PET is a non-invasive technique that images metabolic and biochemical activity at the cellular and molecular level, making it very valuable for early cancer detection and staging, evaluating brain function and identifying heart abnormalities before clear anatomical changes appear.

Medical physics is also very important in the treatment and diagnosis of cancer, especially through radiotherapy, which uses high-energy radiation to kill tumour cells with minimal harm to healthy tissue. Radiation therapy has two main approaches: teletherapy, in which radiation is delivered from a machine outside the body, and brachytherapy, in which a radioactive source is placed inside or close to the tumour. Medical physicists are part of the oncology team: they specialise in equipment quality assurance, calculating treatment times, planning treatment and mapping the dose distribution in the cancerous region, working with radiation oncologists, dosimetrists and laboratory technicians to make every treatment safe and effective.
